newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya donors urge Moi to pursue dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Kenya donors urge Moi to pursue dialogue.

text.p: Kenya's donors have urged President Daniel arap Moi to pursue dialogue with the opposition to avoid further political violence.

Diplomats in a letter praised Moi for "demonstrating leadership" by meeting opposition and church leaders last week and said they supported Moi's directive that requests for political meetings be granted automatically.
Diplomats have stepped up pressure on Moi, aged 73 and in power since 1978, since at least nine people were killed when police moved in on July 7 to crush rallies in support of constitutional reform.
The letter was written on Thursday by Canadian High Commissioner Bernard Dussault on behalf of 22 embassies and high commissioners in the Donor Democratic Development Group.
The group, formed to coordinate the diplomatic approach to the last elections in 1992, includes European Union countries, the United States, Japan and the Czech Republic.

"Dialogue is not easy, particularly on such difficult issues where different views are deeply held. Nevertheless we believe that open and frank dialogue is the only way to achieve durable progress," said the letter, whose contents were read to Reuters.

The directive on political meetings was "an initiative to break the increasingly dangerous dynamic of provocation and reaction that has recently tainted Kenya's politcs and resulted in the violent deaths of innocent Kenyans which so shocked the international community".
Britain said on Wednesday it would reduce aid to Kenya if the government continued to crack down on demands for constitutional change.
The ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) last week announced it would set up a commission to review the constitution and recommended the repeal of 11 laws targetted by the reform campaign.

But KANU said it would talk only to elected representatives and not to the National Convention Executive Council (NCEC), an opposition-backed group spearheading a campaign for reforms before elections due by the end of 1997. No election date has been set.
Diplomats stressed they were not attempting to put pressure on Moi over reforms.
"This is just the international community weighing in saying -- you have started on the right path and just keep going," one Western diplomat told Reuters.

"People question Moi's sincerity, but he wants to keep power and he wouldn't be the first leader in the history of the world who is forced to make concessions that then turn out to be really good," the diplomat said.
The NCEC plans to hold a rally on Saturday in Mombasa, Kenya's second city and the centre of its tourism industry, without applying for a licence.
